measures.questionText: Shall the measure, increasing the permissible height of “multiple-family developments” in the City of Coronado’s R-4 Multiple Family Residential Zone from the existing maximum of 3 stories (with a maximum height of no more than 35 feet) to a maximum of 4 stories (with a maximum height of no more than 42 feet), be adopted?
measures.officialStatement:
Impartial City Attorney Analysis of Ballot Masure D

The City Council of the City of Coronado placed Measure D on the ballot for voter
consideration at the November 3, 2026, election.

Coronado Municipal Code (“CMC”) Section 86.56.048 and Section B-2 of Part B of
Chapter V of the Orange Avenue Corridor Specific Plan (“OACSP”) currently limit the
height of multiple-family developments in the R-4 Multiple-Family Residential Zone (“R-4
Zone”) to a maximum building height of three stories with a maximum 35-foot height limit
(“Existing Height Limit”).

As part of the City’s Sixth Cycle Housing Element Update adoption (“Housing Element
Update”), the California Department of Housing and Community Development (“HCD”)
took the position that the Existing Height Limit constitutes a constraint on developments
seeking to obtain the permitted density of 40 dwelling units per acre. Further, per HCD’s
guidance, a zoning district must allow at least one story and 10 feet of height for every 10
dwelling units per acre of density allowed. In other words, the R-4 Zone’s density of 40
dwelling units per acre must correspond with a height limit no lower than 4 stories and 40
feet and HCD has expressed that 42 feet is preferred to avoid constraining the density.
As a result, the Housing Element Update contains Program H.1.F that requires the City to
submit Measure D to the voters.

If approved, Measure D would revise the height limits in both the CMC 86.56.048 and the
OACSP pertaining to multiple family developments in the R-4 Zone so that the maximum
building height is four stories but no more than 42 feet. This revision will be in compliance
with HCD’s requirements stated above.

A “Yes” vote is a vote in favor of Measure D, which is a vote in favor of revising the height
limits as stated above. “No” vote is a vote against Measure D, which is a vote against
revising the height limits as stated above. Measure D will be approved if it receives a
simple majority of “Yes” votes.



Johanna N. Canlas
City Attorney, City of Coronado

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure D. If you desire a copy of the
ordinance or measure, please call the election official ’s office at 619-522-7320 and a
copy will be mailed at no cost to you.

provenance.quote: Shall the measure, increasing the permissible height of “multiple-family developments” in the City of Coronado’s R-4 Multiple Family Residential Zone from the existing maximum of 3 stories (with a maximum height of no more than 35 feet) to a maximum of 4 stories (with a maximum height of no more than 42 feet), be adopted?

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Raise the allowed height of multiple-family development in Coronado’s R-4 Multiple-Family Residential Zone from the current maximum of three stories and 35 feet to four stories. Under the amended Orange Avenue Corridor Specific Plan, flat roofs, including parapets and false mansards, and roofs with a slope below 2:12 could reach 40 feet; roofs with a slope of 2:12 or greater could reach 42 feet. The measure changes both the municipal zoning code and the specific plan. It implements the height change required in the city’s adopted housing-element program. Approval requires a majority vote, and the ordinance takes effect ten days after the council declares the election result.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve these four-story multiple-family height limits in the R-4 zone and the related code and specific-plan amendments.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these proposed height changes; the existing local three-story height rules would remain.

parts.label: Scope and later changes
parts.what: The change applies to multiple-family development in the R-4 zone, rather than citywide building heights. The specific plan keeps separate rules for nonresidential buildings, single-family homes, duplexes and accessory buildings. The existing rule allowing qualifying 90%-transparent cable railings two feet above the otherwise allowed height remains. The council may make administrative amendments that further the ordinance’s purpose, but changes to the height requirements must be approved by voters.
